topic: System-effect (screenline) evaluation of a new link
idea: Judge a new freeway or arterial by the whole corridor, not itself: before and after, compare peak-hour volume to design capacity on each parallel road crossing a screenline (Chicago Congress Expressway: all 11 parallel arterials above ratio 1 in 1959, 3 in 1961; parallel LA arterials fell from 46,000 to 14,000 veh/day), plus secondary increases on intersecting roads (3 of 8 N-S arterials newly above 1). Report the volume-to-capacity ratio per road, travel-time in the heavy direction, and induced vehicle-miles (21% observed against 7% normal growth).
does: Given a set of roads (a screenline) and two runs or scenarios, tabulates peak-hour flow, flow/capacity ratio, change, roads that cross 1.0 in either direction, diverted vehicles, and total vehicle-km change (induced travel) so a new road is judged by corridor and system effects.
inputs: two run ids or experiment scenarios, road ids or auto-selected roads crossing a line/corridor
outputs: table per road: flow before/after, v/c before/after, newly overloaded roads, diverted vehicles, vehicle-km change
cite: Ch 4 Performance of Urban Highway Systems, Tables 22-24 (Chicago, Los Angeles, Boston)
notes: Also supports the elastic-demand idea: Baltimore mean work-trip length rose from 2.6 mi (1926) to 4 (1946) to over 5 as service improved, raising peak-hour capacity need above 20 per cent.

topic: Marginal-lane sizing from the hourly profile
idea: Two lane-capacity definitions: service capacity (1,200-1,700 veh/lane/h at about 45 mph) and maximum volume (1,400-1,900 veh/lane/h at 30-40 mph). Size lanes from the hourly profile: the extra lane is justified by the share of daily volume above N-lane capacity (Lodge-Ford: 12-13% of daily volume above 3,000 veh/h in one direction used a lane costing 16% extra); peak-hour shares range 7.2 to 12.8% of daily volume.
does: Applies the daily profile to each road's demand and reports hours over capacity, share of daily volume served by each additional lane, and the lane count at which marginal lane volume falls below a threshold, under either capacity definition.
inputs: road demand per hour (daily profile), lane capacity definition
outputs: per-lane marginal volume share, hours over capacity, recommended lane count
existing: partial: shape_daily_curve, daily profile; no lane sizing tool
notes: Costs in 1960s dollars; use only the volume-share logic.

topic: CBD cordon analysis: through versus local traffic
idea: Capacity should be judged on the single peak hour and on cordon crossings, not daily capacity (daily figures show 5x more capacity than needed). Through traffic is a large share of what crosses a downtown cordon (Buffalo 60-70%, Milwaukee 30%, New Orleans 78% of inbound 10-18h, Atlanta 57%, Detroit 25% of the evening peak), so a bypass or inner belt cuts central load.
does: Draws a cordon (set of roads or a radius around a junction) and reports, from a run's per-vehicle origin and destination, the peak-hour crossings by mode, the share of vehicles that cross without stopping or having an origin/destination inside (through share), and the flow that a bypass would remove.
inputs: run with vehicle origin, destination, route; cordon definition
outputs: peak-hour inbound/outbound crossings, through share %, local share %, by mode and by road
existing: none (read_traffic gives per-vehicle origin/destination live; no cordon analysis)
cite: Ch 5 Aggregate Demand and Capacity Requirements, Table 25
notes: Counting through traffic needs route lists per vehicle in the run output.

topic: Mode- and purpose-specific peaking, directional imbalance and diversion benchmarks
idea: Benchmarks for demand shape: maximum peak hour share of daily volume bus 16%, rail transit 14-20%, commuter rail up to 25%, highways 7-13%; four peak hours carry 28-72%; flow in the minor direction in the peak hour 13-23% for transit but 36-43% for highways; transit riders are 70-85% work trips and transit shares fall from work to shopping to social-recreation; a new rapid-transit line drew 85-86% of riders from existing transit and only 12-13% from cars.
does: Lets shape_daily_curve and set_od_demand take per-mode and per-purpose peak shares and a directional split, and warns when a built profile is outside these ranges; the diversion figure (12-13% from cars) is a sanity check on choose_modes after a transit improvement.
outputs: daily curves per mode, peak-hour shares, directional flows, plausibility flags
notes: 1950s United States data; use as order-of-magnitude checks only.

topic: Trip-length distribution and mode elasticity benchmarks
idea: Cumulative commute-distance profiles per mode (Chicago: median bus trip 2.2-2.4 mi, rapid transit 6.7 mi, commuter rail 11.5 mi, automobile 12 mi; elapsed time nearly equal across modes so long-haul modes simply go farther) and the share of CBD workers living within a distance (74% within 10 mi Chicago, 84% Detroit). Detroit elasticities of mode share: mean family income +0.21 for car drivers and -0.76 for transit riders; transit service at the workplace +0.31 for transit riders.
does: Computes the cumulative distribution of trip length (and time) by vehicle type from a run's arrived vehicles and compares it with the cumulative distribution implied by the demand or with benchmark shapes (shorter for buses, longer for rail/car); also reports mode-share response to a change in a variable (income, service level) as an elasticity table from experiment scenarios.
inputs: run (per-vehicle distance and time by type), experiment scenarios with changed headway or demand
outputs: cumulative distance/time profile per type, median trip length per type, elasticity of mode share to service change
notes: Based on Chicago and Detroit 1956/1953 surveys (Kain); use for shape checks, not parameters.

topic: Annualised system cost model for comparing designs
idea: Total annual cost TC = alpha*n*U + beta*M + gamma*L + S: U vehicle groups needed, M vehicle-miles (M = 1020*d*r*n*U: 255 workdays x 4 peak hours), L lane- or track-miles, S structure and right-of-way cost (index by width and a function of density), alpha cost per vehicle per period, beta per mile, gamma per lane-mile; capital annualised by CRF = i(1+i)^n/((1+i)^n - 1) (6% opportunity cost; 50-year structures 0.06344, 12-year buses 0.11928). Terminal cost is a step function of arrivals per peak hour (one bus slot per 70 buses/h).
does: Adds a monetary comparison to run_experiment scenarios: annual vehicle cost, running cost per vehicle-km from the run, lane-km of roads added, capital annualised by CRF, plus travel-time cost with a value of time, giving cost per passenger and net benefit against the baseline.
inputs: scenario edits (lane-km, buses), run results (vehicle-km, vehicle-hours), unit costs, interest rate, lives, value of time
outputs: annual cost per category, cost per passenger-trip, net benefit vs baseline, break-even demand
cite: Ch 8 Costing Procedures and Assumptions, Eq (1), (2), (8), Table 57
notes: 1960s unit costs are obsolete; take the structure, with user-supplied or current unit costs.

topic: Fleet and headway sizing for a transit line
idea: Round trips per peak hour R = V/(n*c) (major-direction peak volume V, vehicle capacity c); vehicles needed U = R*t/3600 with round-trip time t = running time + accelerate/decelerate/door time (function of stops) + loading/unloading time (door space and boardings) + turnaround; minimum tolerable rush-hour frequency h imposes R_i >= h at each station, which lowers the load factor if not met; time constraint t <= specified (or an overall speed floor).
does: Given a bus line (route length, stops, demand per peak hour), computes round-trip time, the headway and fleet that meet capacity and the minimum frequency, load factor, and the cost per passenger; sets the timetable (headway_min) for a bus type or tram automatically.
inputs: line route and stops, peak-hour demand in major direction, vehicle capacity, dwell and turnaround times, minimum frequency
outputs: round-trip time, trips per hour, headway, fleet size, load factor, binding constraint
existing: partial: create_vehicle_types / update_vehicle_type (headway_min), add_bus_stop; no sizing tool
notes: Eq (6): t = t1 + t2 + t3 + t4. Fleet needs a maintenance spare factor on top.

topic: Corridor mode screening by volume (indivisibility and crossover)
idea: Unit cost per passenger-trip against one-way peak-hour corridor volume (5,000 to 50,000): surface integrated bus is cheapest below about 20,000 pax/h (50-60% cheaper than auto on surface downtown streets); rail and subways are indivisible (high unit cost at low volume, leveling off near 20,000) and win only at high volume, high density, evenly loaded routes and rising downtown share of the trip; automobile is as cheap as any mode at 5,000-10,000 pax/h and has service advantages; cost rises almost linearly with route length. Lane capacities: grade-separated lane about 1,675 veh/h, bus lane 480 buses/h conservative (720-1100 reported), removing curb parking adds about 1,100 veh/h per mile.
does: For a corridor (demand per hour, length, density) estimates cost and time per passenger for car, bus on mixed traffic, bus lane, and rail using fixed plus variable cost with indivisibility steps, and names the crossover volumes; gives the assistant a prior on which mode or lane treatment to test with run_experiment.
inputs: corridor peak-hour volume, route length, density, unit costs (user-adjustable)
outputs: cost per passenger-trip by mode vs volume, crossover volumes, travel time by mode, recommended modes to simulate
existing: none (choose_modes picks shares; no design screening)
cite: Ch 11 Figures 42-55, Evaluation of Travel Modes for Over-all Transport
notes: Based on 1962 costs; reuse the cost structure and the lane-capacity numbers. Bus time = half the trip time + half the headway + 3 min walk; auto = 15 mph + 2 min parking + 3 min walk.

topic: Lane capacity benchmarks by number of lanes
idea: California freeway study (Webb and Moskowitz 1957): passenger-car lane capacity at 35 mph or more rises with lane count: 1 lane 1000 veh/h, 2 lanes 1000 per lane (3,200 total roadway one direction?), 3 lanes 1600, 4 lanes 1665, 5 or more 1675 per lane; lane-mile requirement = volume per segment / lane capacity rounded up; auto occupancy 1.6-1.9 per car at the rush-hour major direction.
does: Compares each multi-lane road's simulated maximum sustained throughput per lane (from detectors) with the benchmark per lane by lane count, to detect Krauss/LC2013 calibration where lane changing loses capacity on 2-lane roads or inflates it on 4+ lanes.
inputs: run detectors, lane count per road
outputs: observed per-lane capacity vs benchmark by lane count, flag outliers
existing: partial: check_calibration (flows against counts); fit_fundamental_diagram idea
cite: Appendix B Table 66; Ch 9 bus lane 480 buses/h
notes: Table text is garbled by OCR; the 2-lane total (3200) and per-lane values should be re-read from the page image before use.

topic: Feeder bus stop spacing, walking distance and frequency trade-off
idea: Stops placed 2w blocks apart with passengers walking at most w blocks; each stop is served h times per hour, so loading per stop v = p*2w^2/h (p CBD-bound trips per block per hour); area served per line-haul station A = V/p. Raising w from 2 to 3 blocks cut cost about 4 cents per trip at p=2 per block and cut vehicle travel time 20-25%; cost per trip falls with density and flattens near 10 originations per block per hour; minimum frequency h of 6 per hour assumed.
does: For a bus road with demand density (people per hectare from institutions), compute passenger loading per stop, the stop spacing that minimises total passenger time (walk time + half-headway wait + in-vehicle time with a dwell and accel/decel penalty per stop) and bus cost, then place the stops with add_bus_stop and return the trade-off table by walk distance and headway.
inputs: road length, demand density, walk speed, dwell per stop, headway, bus speed
outputs: optimal stop spacing, stops placed, passengers per stop, average passenger door-to-door time, vehicle travel time vs w
existing: partial: add_bus_stop, update_bus_stop, institution_mode_split (assumes 5 min walk to the stop and half headway wait)
notes: Standard block = 1/144 sq mile in the book; convert to metres. Direct tie to the half-headway wait term already used in choose_modes.

topic: Ramp metering against capacity drop (input control)
idea: As entering volume nears maximum capacity, shock waves form and output capacity falls (the delay-volume curve bends backward: output volume drops from Va to Vb and delay grows without bound if input stays at or above Va). Control input so the facility stays at design capacity: a detector on each ramp reports to a master station that integrates mainline flow, predicts flow at bottleneck points and closes selected ramps or reduces inflow proportionally at each entrance (the proposal behind modern ramp metering).
does: An extension (signal_override/algorithm hook) for the interchange slip/ramp junctions that meters or closes ramps when downstream detector occupancy/flow exceeds a threshold of capacity; evaluate with run_experiment against no control, reporting throughput, mean delay and the capacity drop avoided.
inputs: interchange ramps, mainline detectors, flow threshold
outputs: ramp release rate, mainline throughput and delay vs baseline, measured capacity drop
existing: none (build_interchange and add_slip_road exist; no ramp control); related: signal_override extension hook
cite: Ch 12 Possible Bus System Innovations, Figure 57
notes: The 1965 source gives the idea and the shape of the curve only; the capacity-drop size must come from simulated queue discharge rates.

topic: Priority merge and net person-delay test for transit priority
idea: Head-of-line (priority) merge lets buses or emergency vehicles skip the ramp queue using a second ramp lane; accept only if the bus passengers' time saved outweighs the aggregate delay to cars (no single car unduly delayed but the sum can be large when queues are long), i.e. a net passenger-time test using vehicle occupancy (1.5-1.9 persons per car vs a loaded bus). Exclusive bus lanes act like a prohibitive price on cars; reserved bus lane capacity 25,000-30,000 seated passengers/h vs about 3,000 people per car lane. Loading time is 10-30% of bus trip time and close to 60% of trip delays.
does: Computes, for TSP, bus lane or priority-merge decisions, the net person-delay (sum over vehicles of occupancy x delay change) so the LLM agent decides priority by passengers, not vehicles, and reports it for each TSP grant; also an offline analysis from a run comparing bus and car passenger delay with and without priority.
inputs: vehicle occupancy by type, delay per vehicle with and without priority, queue length and arrival rate
outputs: net person-seconds saved or lost, bus passenger gain, car passenger loss, accept/reject
existing: partial: TSP and DEVL agents (live decisions); occupancy is a vehicle-type field
cite: Ch 12 Possible Bus System Innovations, Figure 58, bus lane capacity
notes: The text sets up the worked comparison (1,300 veh/h ramp arrivals, a 2-mile queue at 10 mph) that is cut off in the OCR; the calculation is occupancy-weighted delay. This is a good evaluation signal for the TSP agent and a KPI for read_results.

topic: Marginal congestion cost and peak-capacity pricing
idea: Incremental cost pricing: each user should pay the resource cost of extra capacity plus the congestion cost he imposes (marginal social cost above average cost). Highway incremental cost = physical component plus congestion component; invest until marginal capacity cost equals marginal congestion-cost reduction; peak users pay peak capacity costs. Flow and speed trade: rush hours carry 1,600-1,800 veh/lane/h at 30-35 mph vs 1,500-1,600 at 40-50 mph midday, so peak and off-peak capacity use are closer than flow figures suggest.
does: From a link's simulated speed-flow curve (several demand levels via scale_demand), computes the marginal external travel-time cost per extra vehicle (V * dT/dV) times a value of time, giving the efficient toll per road and hour, the revenue, and whether adding a lane (capacity cost) beats tolling at the margin.
inputs: scenario with demand scaled across a range, link flows and speeds, value of time
outputs: efficient toll per link and hour, average vs marginal cost curve, break-even lane cost per lane-km
existing: none (see set_road_toll idea from Rodrigue; no marginal-cost analysis)
notes: Book is qualitative; the formula t = V*dT/dV is the standard result. It also notes congestion rationing may be more progressive than money tolls (equity consideration for the assistant's report).

topic: Bus stop berth capacity and dwell
idea: Number of bus slots (berths) per incoming lane = (deceleration + loading/unloading + acceleration time) / bus headway per lane; a single slot safely handles about 70 buses per hour with centralised fare collection and triple-door buses; with partial loads or distribution across stations the loading time and so slots required fall. Rail cost uses a 4.2 mph/s deceleration and 0 to 30 mph in 14 s acceleration profile for dwell/clearance.
does: For each bus stop, from timetabled headways (all lines using it) and observed dwell and clearance times in a run, computes berth utilisation, buses per hour against about 3600/(dwell + clearance), and flags stops where bus queues form and spill into the lane.
inputs: bus stops, line headways, dwell times from a run
outputs: utilisation per stop, berths needed, queueing buses, delay caused to following traffic
existing: partial: add_bus_stop / update_bus_stop (bay beside the kerb); not_built lists boarding times and loads as placeholder
cite: Appendix B CBD Terminal Design, Figure 61
notes: Dwell depends on passengers boarding which ACMS does not model (not_built); use a fixed dwell.
